claim: Transient receptor potential canonical (TRPC) proteins form nonselective cation channels that play physiological roles in a wide variety of cells.
source: Transient receptor potential canonical (TRPC) proteins form nonselective cation channels that play physiological roles in a wide variety of cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about TRPC proteins supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: TRPC6 inhibition has therapeutic potential in treating pathological cardiac and renal conditions.
source: Despite growing evidence supporting the therapeutic potential of TRPC6 inhibition in treating pathological cardiac and renal conditions, mechanistic understanding of TRPC6 function and modulation remains obscure.
evidence: The claim references 'growing evidence' which implies citation of prior work, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: The antagonist AM-1473 binds to a cytoplasm-facing pocket formed by S1-S4 and the TRP helix in TRPC6.
source: The antagonist binds to a cytoplasm-facing pocket formed by S1-S4 and the TRP helix, whereas the agonist wedges at the subunit interface between S6 and the pore helix.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure determination and structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The agonist AM-0883 wedges at the subunit interface between S6 and the pore helix in TRPC6.
source: The antagonist binds to a cytoplasm-facing pocket formed by S1-S4 and the TRP helix, whereas the agonist wedges at the subunit interface between S6 and the pore helix.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure determination and structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Several disease-related mutations enhance TRPC6 channel activity by disrupting interfacial interactions.
source: Furthermore, structural and mutagenesis analyses suggest several disease-related mutations enhance channel activity by disrupting interfacial interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by both structural analysis and mutagenesis experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mammalian TRPC subfamily consists of seven transmembrane proteins (TRPC1-7).
source: The mammalian TRPC subfamily consists of seven transmembrane proteins (TRPC1-7) that have been proposed to form non-selective cation channels in various cell types (Clapham et al., 2001; Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TRPC6, TRPC3, and TRPC7 can be directly activated by diacylglycerol (DAG).
source: TRPC6 and its most close homologs TRPC3 and TRPC7 are unique among the TRPCs in that they can be directly activated by second messenger diacylglycerol (DAG) (Hofmann et al., 1999), a product of phospholipase C action.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hofmann et al., 1999.

claim: DAG is a product of phospholipase C action.
source: TRPC6 and its most close homologs TRPC3 and TRPC7 are unique among the TRPCs in that they can be directly activated by second messenger diacylglycerol (DAG) (Hofmann et al., 1999), a product of phospholipase C action.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: TRPC6-mediated cation influx regulates physiological function of pulmonary endothelial cells.
source: TRPC6-mediated cation influx regulates physiological function of pulmonary endothelial cells (Singh et al., 2007), smooth muscle cells (Dietrich et al., 2005) and glomerular podocytes (Reiser et al., 2005), whereas TRPC6 hyperactivity has been implicated in maladaptive tissue and organ remodeling (Reiser et al., 2005; Kuwahara et al., 2006; Onohara et al., 2006; Tian et al., 2010; Xie et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2007.

claim: TRPC6-mediated cation influx regulates physiological function of smooth muscle cells.
source: TRPC6-mediated cation influx regulates physiological function of pulmonary endothelial cells (Singh et al., 2007), smooth muscle cells (Dietrich et al., 2005) and glomerular podocytes (Reiser et al., 2005), whereas TRPC6 hyperactivity has been implicated in maladaptive tissue and organ remodeling (Reiser et al., 2005; Kuwahara et al., 2006; Onohara et al., 2006; Tian et al., 2010; Xie et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dietrich et al., 2005.

claim: TRPC6-mediated cation influx regulates physiological function of glomerular podocytes.
source: TRPC6-mediated cation influx regulates physiological function of pulmonary endothelial cells (Singh et al., 2007), smooth muscle cells (Dietrich et al., 2005) and glomerular podocytes (Reiser et al., 2005), whereas TRPC6 hyperactivity has been implicated in maladaptive tissue and organ remodeling (Reiser et al., 2005; Kuwahara et al., 2006; Onohara et al., 2006; Tian et al., 2010; Xie et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Reiser et al., 2005.

claim: TRPC6 hyperactivity has been implicated in maladaptive tissue and organ remodeling.
source: TRPC6-mediated cation influx regulates physiological function of pulmonary endothelial cells (Singh et al., 2007), smooth muscle cells (Dietrich et al., 2005) and glomerular podocytes (Reiser et al., 2005), whereas TRPC6 hyperactivity has been implicated in maladaptive tissue and organ remodeling (Reiser et al., 2005; Kuwahara et al., 2006; Onohara et al., 2006; Tian et al., 2010; Xie et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Upregulation of TRPC6 in myocytes plays a role in cardiac hypertrophy.
source: Notably, upregulation of TRPC6 in myocytes plays a role in cardiac hypertrophy (Kuwahara et al., 2006; Onohara et al., 2006; Xie et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2010), and gain-of-function mutations of TRPC6 contribute to hereditary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), a renal disorder characterized by podocyte injury and a potential cause of end stage renal disease (Reiser et al., 2005; Heeringa et al., 2009; Ilatovskaya and Staruschenko, 2015; Mottl et al., 2013; Winn et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations of TRPC6 contribute to hereditary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).
source: Notably, upregulation of TRPC6 in myocytes plays a role in cardiac hypertrophy (Kuwahara et al., 2006; Onohara et al., 2006; Xie et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2010), and gain-of-function mutations of TRPC6 contribute to hereditary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), a renal disorder characterized by podocyte injury and a potential cause of end stage renal disease (Reiser et al., 2005; Heeringa et al., 2009; Ilatovskaya and Staruschenko, 2015; Mottl et al., 2013; Winn et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: FSGS is a renal disorder characterized by podocyte injury and a potential cause of end stage renal disease.
source: Notably, upregulation of TRPC6 in myocytes plays a role in cardiac hypertrophy (Kuwahara et al., 2006; Onohara et al., 2006; Xie et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2010), and gain-of-function mutations of TRPC6 contribute to hereditary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), a renal disorder characterized by podocyte injury and a potential cause of end stage renal disease (Reiser et al., 2005; Heeringa et al., 2009; Ilatovskaya and Staruschenko, 2015; Mottl et al., 2013; Winn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TRPC6 emerges as an important therapeutic target for pharmacological inhibition.
source: Due to pathological roles of excessive TRPC6 activity, TRPC6 emerges as an important therapeutic target for pharmacological inhibition (Bon and Beech, 2013; Lin et al., 2019; Seo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Development of potent and selective small-molecule antagonists of TRPC6 is hampered by limited understanding of the molecular mechanism of TRPC6 modulation.
source: However, development of potent and selective small-molecule antagonists of TRPC6 is hampered by limited understanding of the molecular mechanism of TRPC6 modulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the state of the field at the time of writing.

claim: Recent cryo-EM structures of several TRPC channels elucidate their tetrameric assembly comprising a transmembrane domain and a cytoplasmic domain.
source: Recent cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of several TRPC channels elucidate their tetrameric assembly comprising a transmembrane domain and a cytoplasmic domain (Azumaya et al., 2018; Duan et al., 2019; Duan et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2018; Sierra-Valdez et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2018; Vinayagam et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior structural studies.

claim: One antagonist-binding site has been identified in human TRPC6.
source: Despite identification of one antagonist-binding site in human TRPC6 (Tang et al., 2018) and multiple lipid-binding sites in human TRPC3 and mouse TRPC5 (Duan et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2018) molecular contacts with the antagonist are not well defined because of limited resolution, and the function of observed lipids remains to be determined (Duan et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2018.

claim: Multiple lipid-binding sites have been identified in human TRPC3 and mouse TRPC5.
source: Despite identification of one antagonist-binding site in human TRPC6 (Tang et al., 2018) and multiple lipid-binding sites in human TRPC3 and mouse TRPC5 (Duan et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2018) molecular contacts with the antagonist are not well defined because of limited resolution, and the function of observed lipids remains to be determined (Duan et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Duan et al., 2019 and Fan et al., 2018.

claim: Molecular contacts with the antagonist in TRPC6 are not well defined because of limited resolution in previous structures.
source: Despite identification of one antagonist-binding site in human TRPC6 (Tang et al., 2018) and multiple lipid-binding sites in human TRPC3 and mouse TRPC5 (Duan et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2018) molecular contacts with the antagonist are not well defined because of limited resolution, and the function of observed lipids remains to be determined (Duan et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on evaluation of prior structural studies.

claim: There is no TRPC structure with a known agonist prior to this study.
source: Furthermore, since there is no TRPC structure with a known agonist, it is still elusive how TRPC channels are activated by DAG or other agonists.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on knowledge of prior literature.

claim: The mechanism of TRPC channel activation by DAG or other agonists is elusive.
source: Furthermore, since there is no TRPC structure with a known agonist, it is still elusive how TRPC channels are activated by DAG or other agonists.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of structural data.

claim: Two high-resolution cryo-EM structures of antagonist- and agonist-bound human TRPC6 in lipidic nanodiscs were determined.
source: In this study, we present two high-resolution cryo-EM structures of antagonist- and agonist-bound human TRPC6 in lipidic nanodiscs.
evidence: This is the primary experimental result of the manuscript.

claim: The structures identify two novel modulation sites in the transmembrane domain of TRPC6.
source: Our structures identify two novel modulation sites in the transmembrane domain and reveal the binding modes of the small molecule antagonist and agonist, which were corroborated by functional data.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and functional validation.

claim: The binding modes of the small molecule antagonist and agonist were corroborated by functional data.
source: Our structures identify two novel modulation sites in the transmembrane domain and reveal the binding modes of the small molecule antagonist and agonist, which were corroborated by functional data.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and functional assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Residues 2-72 of TRPC6 are missing in TRPC3.
source: An N-terminally truncated (Δ2–72) human TRPC6 was engineered because residues corresponding to 2–72 of TRPC6 are missing in TRPC3 despite high overall sequence similarity between TRPC3 and TRPC6.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison between TRPC3 and TRPC6.

claim: TRPC6 (Δ2–72) showed enhanced biochemical stability.
source: TRPC6 (Δ2–72) showed enhanced biochemical stability and could be activated by oleoyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycerol (OAG), a soluble analog of the native lipid agonist DAG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: TRPC6 (Δ2–72) could be activated by oleoyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycerol (OAG).
source: TRPC6 (Δ2–72) showed enhanced biochemical stability and could be activated by oleoyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycerol (OAG), a soluble analog of the native lipid agonist DAG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: OAG is a soluble analog of the native lipid agonist DAG.
source: TRPC6 (Δ2–72) showed enhanced biochemical stability and could be activated by oleoyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycerol (OAG), a soluble analog of the native lipid agonist DAG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about OAG.

claim: AM-1473 is a small molecule antagonist with an IC50 of 0.22 ± 0.05 nM (n = 14) in the TRPC6 bioassay.
source: AM-1473, a small molecule antagonist with an IC50 of 0.22 ± 0.05 nM (n = 14) in our TRPC6 bioassay, is a structural analog of previously disclosed small molecule antagonist SAR-7334 (Maier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is experimental data from the bioassay performed in the study.

claim: AM-1473 is a structural analog of SAR-7334.
source: AM-1473, a small molecule antagonist with an IC50 of 0.22 ± 0.05 nM (n = 14) in our TRPC6 bioassay, is a structural analog of previously disclosed small molecule antagonist SAR-7334 (Maier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on chemical structure comparison and citation to prior work.

claim: AM-0883 is a novel TRPC6 agonist with an EC50 of 45.5 ± 10 nM (n = 19).
source: AM-0883, a novel TRPC6 agonist with an EC50 of 45.5 ± 10 nM (n = 19) was identified from a small molecule in vitro high throughput screening campaign at Amgen.
evidence: This is experimental data from the bioassay performed in the study.

claim: AM-0883 was identified from a small molecule in vitro high throughput screening campaign at Amgen.
source: AM-0883, a novel TRPC6 agonist with an EC50 of 45.5 ± 10 nM (n = 19) was identified from a small molecule in vitro high throughput screening campaign at Amgen.
evidence: This describes the method of discovery of the compound.

claim: TRPC6 (Δ2–72) could be inhibited by AM-1473 with an IC50 of 0.13 ± 0.03 nM (n = 5).
source: Similar to the WT protein, TRPC6 (Δ2–72) could be inhibited by AM-1473 (IC50 = 0.13 ± 0.03 nM, n = 5, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c) and activated by AM-0883 (EC50 = 90.2 ± 13 nM, n = 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: TRPC6 (Δ2–72) could be activated by AM-0883 with an EC50 of 90.2 ± 13 nM (n = 4).
source: Similar to the WT protein, TRPC6 (Δ2–72) could be inhibited by AM-1473 (IC50 = 0.13 ± 0.03 nM, n = 5, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c) and activated by AM-0883 (EC50 = 90.2 ± 13 nM, n = 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: The structure of the antagonist-bound TRPC6 in nanodiscs was determined at a resolution of 3.1 Å using single-particle cryo-EM.
source: The structure of the antagonist-bound TRPC6 in nanodiscs was determined at a resolution of 3.1 Å using single-particle cryo-EM (Figure 1, Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is the primary structural result supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: The overall architecture of the antagonist-bound TRPC6 is similar to previous cryo-EM structures of TRPC3 and TRPC6.
source: The overall architecture of the antagonist-bound TRPC6 is similar to previous cryo-EM structures of TRPC3 and TRPC6 (Fan et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior structures.

claim: The voltage-sensor-like domain (S1-S4) and the pore domain (S5-S6) are arranged in a domain-swapped manner in TRPC6.
source: The voltage-sensor-like domain (S1-S4) and the pore domain (S5-S6) are arranged in a domain-swapped manner (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 1.

claim: S3 extends substantially into the extracellular space in TRPC6.
source: S3 extends substantially into the extracellular space (Figure 1a,c).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 1a,c.

claim: An elbow-like structural component is embedded in the lipid bilayer and makes hydrophobic contacts with the intracellular half of S1 in TRPC6.
source: An elbow-like structural component is embedded in the lipid bilayer and makes hydrophobic contacts with the intracellular half of S1 (Figure 1a,c).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 1a,c.

claim: The intracellular domain is assembled through interactions between the ankyrin repeat domain (ARD) at the N-terminus and the rib helix and coiled-coil at the C-terminus.
source: The intracellular domain is assembled through interactions between the ankyrin repeat domain (ARD) at the N-terminus and the rib helix and coiled-coil at the C-terminus (Figure 1a,c).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 1a,c.

claim: The antagonist AM-1473 consists of an aminopiperidine, a benzonitrile, and an indane.
source: There are several non-protein densities in our cryo-EM map (Figure 1). Based on the shape and chemical environment, it is very likely that the density within the pocket of S1-S4 observed in the final postprocessed map and two corresponding half-maps belongs to the antagonist AM-1473 (Figure 1c–d, Figure 2a–b, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2f–h), which consists of an aminopiperidine, a benzonitrile, and an indane (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on the chemical structure of AM-1473 shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The S1-S4 pocket was empty in the structure of TRPC6 bound to BTDM.
source: Furthermore, this pocket was empty in the structure of TRPC6 bound to another small molecule antagonist BTDM (Tang et al., 2018) or the TRPC3 structure (Tang et al., 2018; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), further supporting our assignment of the density to the antagonist.
evidence: This is based on comparison with a prior structure from Tang et al., 2018.

claim: The primary amine moiety off the piperidine ring of AM-1473 forms hydrogen-bond interactions with Glu509 on S2 and Asp530 on S3.
source: The primary amine moiety off the piperidine ring forms hydrogen-bond interactions with Glu509 on S2, and Asp530 on S3.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure showing specific molecular interactions.

claim: The benzonitrile group of AM-1473 is involved in a cation-π interaction with Arg758 on the reentrant loop.
source: The benzonitrile group is involved in a cation-π interaction with Arg758 on the reentrant loop as well as aromatic-stacking interactions with His446 on S1 and Tyr753 on the TRP helix.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure showing specific molecular interactions.

claim: The benzonitrile group of AM-1473 has aromatic-stacking interactions with His446 on S1 and Tyr753 on the TRP helix.
source: The benzonitrile group is involved in a cation-π interaction with Arg758 on the reentrant loop as well as aromatic-stacking interactions with His446 on S1 and Tyr753 on the TRP helix.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure showing specific molecular interactions.

claim: The indene double ring of AM-1473 makes van der Waal contacts with Tyr612 on S4.
source: The indene double ring makes van der Waal contacts with Tyr612 on S4.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure showing specific molecular interactions.

claim: The antagonist AM-1473 is 36-fold selective for TRPC6 over TRPC3.
source: Interestingly, the antagonist is 36-fold selective for TRPC6 over its closely-related homolog TRPC3 (IC50 of 8.0 ± 2.2 nM, n = 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is experimental data from bioassays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Arg758 on TRPC6 is replaced by a lysine on TRPC3.
source: Among the residues that interact with the antagonist, most are identical between TRPC3 and TRPC6, but Arg758 on TRPC6 is replaced by a lysine on TRPC3.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison between TRPC3 and TRPC6.

claim: The antagonist AM-1473 is 5-fold less potent in TRPC6 R758K mutant.
source: We tested whether exchange this residue between TRPC6 and TRPC3 would have any effect on the antagonist potency and found that the antagonist is 5-fold less potent in TRPC6 R758K and 3.5-fold more potent in TRPC3 K689R (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The antagonist AM-1473 is 3.5-fold more potent in TRPC3 K689R mutant.
source: We tested whether exchange this residue between TRPC6 and TRPC3 would have any effect on the antagonist potency and found that the antagonist is 5-fold less potent in TRPC6 R758K and 3.5-fold more potent in TRPC3 K689R (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lower antagonist potency in TRPC3 could be partly due to the less optimal position for the lysine to form the cation-π interaction with the benzonitrile group.
source: Therefore, we propose that the lower antagonist potency in TRPC3 could be partly due to the less optimal position for the lysine to form the cation-π interaction with the benzonitrile group.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and mutagenesis data.

claim: Mutations E509A and D530A almost completely abolished the response of TRPC6 to the antagonist AM-1473.
source: Mutations that removed the negatively charged residues that interact with the primary amine, E509A and D530A, almost completely abolished the response of TRPC6 to the antagonist, consistent with the critical roles of the negatively charged side chains in ligand recognition and the positively charged primary amine in maintaining antagonist potency (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Mutation R609A lowered the binding affinity of AM-1473 by ~10 fold.
source: Interestingly, mutation R609A, which disrupts the salt-bridge interaction between Arg609 and Asp530, also lowered the binding affinity of compound by ~10 fold (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Mutation R758A lowered the binding affinity of AM-1473 by ~300 fold.
source: Mutation R758A, which disrupts the cation-π interaction, lowered the binding affinity by ~300 fold (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Mutations K442A and N527A lowered the binding-affinity of AM-1473 by ~15 fold.
source: Mutations K442A and N527A lowered the binding-affinity by ~15 fold, suggesting that Lys442 and Gln527 might be involved in hydrophilic interactions with the nitrile and the primary amine, respectively (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Multiple outer leaflet lipids line the membrane-facing crevices between adjacent subunits in TRPC6.
source: Similar to other TRP channels and voltage-gated ion channels, multiple outer leaflet lipids line the membrane-facing crevices between adjacent subunits, making contacts with helices S3-S6 as well as the pore helix (Figure 1a,c).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 1a,c.

claim: One inner leaflet lipid in TRPC6 is buried in a pocket formed by S1, S4 and the pre-S1 elbow, and its size and shape fit well with that of a cholesterol hemisuccinate (CHS) molecule.
source: In the inner leaflet, one lipid is buried in a pocket formed by S1, S4 and the pre-S1 elbow, and its size and shape fit well with that of a cholesterol hemisuccinate (CHS) molecule (Hughes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure with inference about lipid identity based on shape and citation to prior work.

claim: Another inner leaflet lipid in TRPC6 is wedged between S4 and the S4-S5 linker and can be interpreted as a phosphatidylcholine lipid.
source: Another inner leaflet lipid is wedged between S4 and the S4-S5 linker and can be interpreted as a phosphatidylcholine lipid (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure with inference about lipid identity.

claim: The intracellular cleft between S4 and S5 could be a site for channel modulation in TRPC6.
source: Intriguingly, this cleft also contributes to the putative binding site of another small-molecule antagonist of TRPC6 (Tang et al., 2018; Figure 2—figure supplement 3b). Therefore, the intracellular cleft between S4 and S5 could be a site for channel modulation in TRPC6.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison with prior work.

claim: The vanilloid-binding site located near S4 and S5 in TRPV1 accommodates a phosphatidylinositol lipid that could be displaced by vanilloid agonists or antagonists.
source: For example, the vanilloid-binding site located near S4 and S5 in TRPV1 accommodates a phosphatidylinositol lipid that could be displaced by vanilloid agonists or antagonists (Gao et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 3d–e).
evidence: This is based on citation to prior structural work on TRPV1.

claim: In TRPV5, econazole occupies a site similar to the vanilloid-binding site in TRPV1.
source: In TRPV5, econazole, a small molecule antagonist and antifungal, was found to occupy a similar site (Hughes et al., 2018; Figure 2—figure supplement 3f), whereas in TRPV6, native lipids that might be involved in channel activation were identified in this pocket (McGoldrick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citation to prior structural work on TRPV5.

claim: Many disease-related mutations found in FSGS patients are clustered at the region where the N-terminal ARD and the C-terminal rib helix and coiled-coil interact with each other.
source: With the structure, we studied the location of disease-related mutations found in FSGS patients (Mottl et al., 2013). Intriguingly, many of these mutation sites are clustered at the region where the N-terminal ARD and the C-terminal rib helix and coiled-coil interact with each other (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis of disease mutations.

claim: Six mutations (G109S, P112Q, N143S, Q889K, R895C, and E897K) are located at the interface between the ARD and the pole helix of the same subunit.
source: Six mutations, including G109S, P112Q, N143S, Q889K, R895C, and E897K, are located at the interface between the ARD and the pole helix of the same subunit (Figure 3b, interface 1).
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Mutation M132T is located at the interface between the ARD of one subunit and the rib helix of the adjacent subunit.
source: Another mutation, M132T, is located at the interface between the ARD of one subunit and the rib helix of the adjacent subunit (Figure 3b, interface 2).
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Several mutations at interface 1 (positions 109, 112, 889, and 895) led to enhanced channel activity without affecting the expression level on the membrane.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Heeringa et al., 2009; Mottl et al., 2013; Winn et al., 2005), we found several mutations at interface 1, including those at positions 109, 112, 889, and 895, led to enhanced channel activity without affecting the expression level on the membrane (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis and expression studies.

claim: The interactions at interface 1 are important for the stability of the closed state of TRPC6.
source: Since mutations at these positions destabilize the interactions at interface 1, the increased activity in mutant channels suggests that these interactions are important for the stability of the closed state of the channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutagenesis data.

claim: M132T is a disease-causing mutation that increases TRPC6 channel activity.
source: To further explore this idea, we tested whether disrupting the interfacial interactions at interface 2 would have an effect on channel activity. M132T is a disease-causing mutation that also increases channel activity (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Met132 forms hydrophobic interactions with Val867 and Leu868 on the rib helix.
source: In our structure, Met132 forms hydrophobic interactions with Val867 and Leu868 on the rib helix.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: Substitution of either Val867 or Leu868 with a threonine increased maximum channel activity by ~50%.
source: Substitution of either Val867 or Leu868 with a threonine increased maximum channel activity by ~50%, whereas mutating both residues simultaneously more than doubled maximum channel activity (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Mutating both Val867 and Leu868 simultaneously more than doubled maximum channel activity.
source: Substitution of either Val867 or Leu868 with a threonine increased maximum channel activity by ~50%, whereas mutating both residues simultaneously more than doubled maximum channel activity (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The interactions at interface 2 are involved in stabilizing the closed state of TRPC6.
source: Since none of these mutations have any significant effect on the expression level on the membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), the increased channel activity of these mutant channels suggests that the interactions at interface 2 are also involved in stabilizing the closed state of TRPC6.
evidence: This is an inference based on mutagenesis and expression data.

claim: The structure of agonist-bound TRPC6 (Δ2–72) V867T/L868T was determined at 3.1 Å resolution.
source: To understand agonist binding and channel activation, we purified the double mutant TRPC6 (Δ2–72) V867T/L868T channel in complex with the small molecule agonist AM-0883, reconstituted it into nanodiscs and determined the cryo-EM structure at 3.1 Å (Figure 4, Table 1 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is the primary structural result for the agonist-bound state.

claim: AM-0883 induced about the same level of maximum activity as OAG.
source: AM-0883 induced about the same level of maximum activity as OAG, but was ~70 fold more potent than OAG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is experimental data from bioassays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: AM-0883 was ~70 fold more potent than OAG.
source: AM-0883 induced about the same level of maximum activity as OAG, but was ~70 fold more potent than OAG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is experimental data from bioassays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: The low potency of OAG might explain the lack of OAG density in the previous structure of TRPC3 copurified with OAG.
source: We reasoned that the low potency of OAG might explain the lack of OAG density in the previous structure of TRPC3 copurified with OAG (Tang et al., 2018), and the higher potency of AM-0883 would allow us to obtain the agonist-bound structure of TRPC6.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of potencies and prior structural work.

claim: TRPC6 V867T/L868T exhibited much higher channel activity than WT.
source: Furthermore, because TRPC6 V867T/L868T, like WT, responded to both AM-0883 and OAG but exhibited much higher channel activity than WT (Figure 3d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f), the double mutant appeared to be an ideal variant for us to investigate the more activated state of TRPC6.
evidence: This is experimental data from bioassays.

claim: The agonist AM-0883 consists of a chloro-indole, a piperidine and a benzodioxin.
source: We found a clear non-protein density at each subunit interface that represents the agonist AM-0883, which consists of a chloro-indole, a piperidine and a benzodioxin, and occupies a groove between S6 of one subunit and the pore helix of the adjacent subunit (Figure 4b–c and Figure 5a–b).
evidence: This is based on the chemical structure of AM-0883 and structural analysis.

claim: The agonist AM-0883 occupies a groove between S6 of one subunit and the pore helix of the adjacent subunit.
source: We found a clear non-protein density at each subunit interface that represents the agonist AM-0883, which consists of a chloro-indole, a piperidine and a benzodioxin, and occupies a groove between S6 of one subunit and the pore helix of the adjacent subunit (Figure 4b–c and Figure 5a–b).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: The agonist AM-0883 forms hydrophobic interactions with Phe675 and TRP680 on the pore helix and Tyr705, Val706 and Val710 on S6.
source: The agonist forms hydrophobic interactions with Phe675 and TRP680 on the pore helix and Tyr705, Val706 and Val710 on S6 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 5c.

claim: There are possible hydrophilic interactions between the indole ring of AM-0883 and Glu672 and Asn702.
source: There are also possible hydrophilic interactions between the indole ring and Glu672 and Asn702 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Mutations F675A, W680A, N702A, Y705A and V710A almost completely abolished the channel activity in the presence of the agonist AM-0883.
source: We tested whether mutations around this region would affect the potency of the agonist and found that mutations F675A, W680A, N702A, Y705A and V710A almost completely abolished the channel activity in the presence of the agonist AM-0883, whereas mutations E672A and V706A showed a 35-fold and 20-fold increase in agonist EC50, respectively (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Mutations E672A and V706A showed a 35-fold and 20-fold increase in agonist EC50, respectively.
source: We tested whether mutations around this region would affect the potency of the agonist and found that mutations F675A, W680A, N702A, Y705A and V710A almost completely abolished the channel activity in the presence of the agonist AM-0883, whereas mutations E672A and V706A showed a 35-fold and 20-fold increase in agonist EC50, respectively (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Gly640 on S6 of TRPC3, corresponding to Gly709 of TRPC6, has been proposed as a critical structural component for DAG recognition.
source: Several residues around the agonist-binding site have been shown to affect channel activation by the native lipid agonist DAG. Gly640 on S6 of TRPC3, conserved among TRPCs and corresponding to Gly709 of TRPC6, has been proposed as a critical structural component for DAG recognition (Lichtenegger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citation to prior work by Lichtenegger et al., 2018.

claim: Mutations of Gly640 in TRPC3 and TRPC6 dramatically reduced DAG sensitivity.
source: Mutations of this glycine in TRPC3 and TRPC6 dramatically reduced DAG sensitivity (Hofmann et al., 2002; Strübing et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior work.

claim: The conserved LFW motif (residues 678–680 in TRPC6) on the pore helix has been identified to be essential for channel activation.
source: On the pore helix, the conserved LFW motif (residues 678–680 in TRPC6) has been identified to be essential for channel activation (Hofmann et al., 2002; Strübing et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior work.

claim: Substitution of all three residues of the LFW motif with alanine in TRPC5 and TRPC6 resulted in nonfunctional channels without altering plasma membrane expression.
source: Substitution of all three residues with alanine in TRPC5 and TRPC6 resulted in nonfunctional channels without altering plasma membrane expression (Strübing et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on citation to prior work by Strübing et al., 2003.

claim: Mutations E672A, F675A, W680A, N702A, Y705A and V706A completely eliminated the response to OAG even at a 100 μM concentration.
source: Consistent with the idea that the agonist-binding site is also important for DAG recognition, mutations around the site, including E672A, F675A, W680A, N702A, Y705A and V706A, maintained normal membrane surface expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) but completely eliminated the response to OAG even at a 100 μM concentration (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Glu672 and Val706 appeared to be more critical for the binding of DAG than AM-0883.
source: Furthermore, Glu672 and Val706 appeared to be more critical for the binding of DAG than AM-0883, because channels with mutation E672A or V706A could still be activated by the agonist AM-0883 at reduced potency but not by DAG (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is an inference based on differential effects of mutations on AM-0883 vs DAG activation.

claim: The V710A mutation reduced the maximal activation by OAG by >80%.
source: The V710A mutation also reduced the maximal activation by OAG by >80% (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Among six TRPC proteins found in human, only TRPC3, TRPC6 and TRPC7 are directly activated by DAG.
source: Importantly, among six TRPC proteins found in human, only the closely-related subgroup of TRPC3, TRPC6 and TRPC7 are directly activated by DAG (Hofmann et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on citation to prior work and established knowledge.

claim: Glu672, Asn702 and Tyr705 are only conserved among TRPC3, TRPC6 and TRPC7.
source: Indeed, whereas several residues around the putative DAG-recognition site are conserved across TRPCs, Glu672, Asn702 and Tyr705 are only conserved among TRPC3, TRPC6 and TRPC7 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The AM-0883-binding site faces membrane lipids and is occupied by one of the outer leaflet lipids in the antagonist-bound structure.
source: Notably, the AM-0883-binding site faces membrane lipids and is occupied by one of the outer leaflet lipids in the antagonist-bound structure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,c), and therefore constitutes a likely location for DAG-binding at the outer leaflet.
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison.

claim: The agonist-binding site identified in this study may overlap with the DAG-recognition site.
source: The overall findings strongly suggest that the agonist-binding site identified here may overlap with the DAG-recognition site.
evidence: This is an inference based on mutagenesis data and structural analysis.

claim: Analogous sites near the subunit interface between S6 and the pore helix have been previously identified to accommodate a small molecule agonist in TRPML1.
source: Analogous sites near the subunit interface between S6 and the pore helix have been previously identified to accommodate a small molecule agonist in TRPML1 (Schmiege et al., 2017), and a small molecule antagonist in CavAb (Tang et al., 2016; Figure 5—figure supplement 3), corroborating the important role of this site in channel modulation.
evidence: This is based on citations to prior structural work.

claim: Analogous sites near the subunit interface between S6 and the pore helix have been previously identified to accommodate a small molecule antagonist in CavAb.
source: Analogous sites near the subunit interface between S6 and the pore helix have been previously identified to accommodate a small molecule agonist in TRPML1 (Schmiege et al., 2017), and a small molecule antagonist in CavAb (Tang et al., 2016; Figure 5—figure supplement 3), corroborating the important role of this site in channel modulation.
evidence: This is based on citations to prior structural work.

claim: The double mutant V867T/L868T exhibited a 2-fold increase in maximum activity in the presence of the agonist AM-0883 compared to WT.
source: Compared to the WT protein, the double mutant V867T/L868T exhibited a 2-fold increase in maximum activity in the presence of the agonist AM-0883 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is experimental data from bioassays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: The agonist-bound structure of TRPC6 (Δ2–72) V867T/L868T possesses a closed ion channel pore.
source: However, similar to the antagonist-bound structure of TRPC6 (Δ2–72), the agonist-bound structure of TRPC6 (Δ2–72) V867T/L868T also possesses a closed ion channel pore (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mutations and the agonist were not sufficient to shift the gating equilibrium towards a stable open state.
source: Therefore, the mutations and the agonist were not sufficient to shift the gating equilibrium towards a stable open state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the pore is closed in the agonist-bound structure.

claim: The low open probability and the short open time (<1 ms) of TRPC6 suggest that the closed state is much more energetically stable compared to the open state.
source: This is not surprising because the low open probability and the short open time (<1 ms) of TRPC6 (Hofmann et al., 1999) suggest that the closed state is much more energetically stable compared to the open state.
evidence: This is an inference based on biophysical properties cited from prior work.

claim: The ion permeation pathway in the structures is sealed off by hydrophobic side chains of Leu723, Ile727 and Phe731 near the intracellular end of S6.
source: The ion permeation pathway in our structures is sealed off by hydrophobic side chains of Leu723, Ile727 and Phe731 near the intracellular end of S6 (Figure 6a–b), which are at equivalent positions in TRPC3 as shown in the human TRPC3 structure (Fan et al., 2018), but shifted by one amino acid in the previous human TRPC6 structure (Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: Main chain carbonyls of Phe683 and Gly684 located after the pore helix define the selectivity filter in TRPC6.
source: In both our structures, main chain carbonyls of Phe683 and Gly684 located after the pore helix define the selectivity filter and coordinate a putative cation bound to the selectivity filter (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: The intracellular domain is nearly identical in both antagonist-bound and agonist-bound structures.
source: Although the ion channel pore is closed and the intracellular domain is nearly identical in both our structures (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), there are significant conformational changes in the transmembrane domain associated with ligand binding.
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are significant conformational changes in the transmembrane domain associated with ligand binding.
source: Although the ion channel pore is closed and the intracellular domain is nearly identical in both our structures (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), there are significant conformational changes in the transmembrane domain associated with ligand binding.
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison.

claim: In the ligand-free S1-S4 pocket of the agonist-bound state, the side chain of H446 adopts two alternative rotameric conformations.
source: In the ligand-free S1-S4 pocket of the agonist-bound state, the side chain of H446 adopts two alternative rotameric conformations, one of which occupies the position where the indene double ring of the antagonist would bind, and the side chain of R758 occupies the position where the benzonitrile group of the antagonist would bind (Figure 7—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Side chain movements of H446 and R758 are necessary to accommodate the antagonist.
source: Therefore, side chain movements of H446 and R758 are necessary to accommodate the antagonist.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: Agonist-binding occurs without major structural changes in the side chains of the agonist-binding pocket.
source: On the other hand, agonist-binding occurs without major structural changes in the side chains of the agonist-binding pocket (Figure 7—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The presence of the agonist tilts the extracellular half of S6 away from the pore and pushes S6 toward the intracellular side.
source: Instead, the presence of the agonist seems to tilt the extracellular half of S6 away from the pore and pushes S6 toward the intracellular side (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The movement of S6 is accompanied by a concurrent tilting and downward movement of S1-S4 as well as the S4-S5 linker.
source: Because S6 is tightly packed against S1-S4 of the adjacent subunit, the movement of S6 is accompanied by a concurrent tilting and downward movement of S1-S4 as well as the S4-S5 linker (Figure 7a,c).
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison shown in Figure 7a,c.

claim: S3 has the largest movement among the transmembrane helices, with its extracellular end moving 4.4 Å.
source: Among the transmembrane helices, S3 has the largest movement, with its extracellular end moving 4.4 Å, partly due to the remarkably long extension of S3 into the extracellular side.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from structural comparison.

claim: Agonist binding is accompanied by a counterclockwise rotation around the central ion pathway when viewed from the cytoplasmic side.
source: Viewing from the cytoplasmic side, agonist binding is accompanied by a counterclockwise rotation around the central ion pathway (Figure 7b), resulting in a movement of 2.4–3.3 Å at the intracellular end of S1-S4.
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Agonist binding results in a movement of 2.4–3.3 Å at the intracellular end of S1-S4.
source: Viewing from the cytoplasmic side, agonist binding is accompanied by a counterclockwise rotation around the central ion pathway (Figure 7b), resulting in a movement of 2.4–3.3 Å at the intracellular end of S1-S4.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from structural comparison shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Agonist-bound channels may transition to the open conformation when further counterclockwise rotation of the S6 helical bundle fully unwinds the hydrophobic seal at the intracellular gate.
source: While the structural changes from the antagonist-bound state to the agonist-bound state were not sufficient to stabilize an open channel pore, it is possible that agonist-bound channels may transition to the open conformation when further counterclockwise rotation of the S6 helical bundle fully unwinds the hydrophobic seal at the intracellular gate (Video 1).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed conformational changes.

claim: The AM-1473-bound TRPC6 and the BTDM-bound TRPC6 assume a nearly identical conformation.
source: We found that the AM-1473-bound TRPC6 and the BTDM-bound TRPC6 assume a nearly identical conformation (Figure 7d, Figure 7—figure supplement 1b, Cα-RMSD 0.588), with S1-S4 and the S4-S5 linker in the slightly up conformation, distinct from the slightly down conformation in agonist-bound structure.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior structure from Tang et al., 2018.

claim: The structure of TRPC3 is very similar to the AM-1473-bound and BTDM-bound TRPC6 structures.
source: The structure of TRPC3, which shares ~75% sequence identity with TRPC6, is also very similar to the AM-1473-bound and BTDM-bound TRPC6 structures (Figure 7e and Figure 7—figure supplement 1c, Cα-RMSD 0.710), suggesting that both antagonists may allosterically inhibit the opening of the channel pore by stabilizing the apo or resting state, as observed in the action of antagonists on P2X3 receptor channels and TRPM4 channels (Huang et al., 2020; Mansoor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with prior TRPC3 structure.

claim: Both antagonists may allosterically inhibit the opening of the channel pore by stabilizing the apo or resting state.
source: The structure of TRPC3, which shares ~75% sequence identity with TRPC6, is also very similar to the AM-1473-bound and BTDM-bound TRPC6 structures (Figure 7e and Figure 7—figure supplement 1c, Cα-RMSD 0.710), suggesting that both antagonists may allosterically inhibit the opening of the channel pore by stabilizing the apo or resting state, as observed in the action of antagonists on P2X3 receptor channels and TRPM4 channels (Huang et al., 2020; Mansoor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison and analogy to other channels.

claim: The S1-S4 pocket in TRPC channels could be a site for channel modulation.
source: Since this pocket was empty in all other TRPC structures determined so far (Duan et al., 2019; Duan et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2018; Vinayagam et al., 2018), our structure of the antagonist-bound TRPC6 provides the first evidence that the S1-S4 pocket in TRPC channels could be a site for channel modulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current structure and comparison with prior structures.

claim: The crevice between the S2-S3 linker and the TRP helix connects the S1-S4 pocket to the cytoplasm and provides a possible access route for the antagonist.
source: Notably, the crevice between the S2-S3 linker and the TRP helix connects the pocket to the cytoplasm and provides a possible access route for the antagonist.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: TRPC6 is activated through a unique mechanism compared to TRPV and TRPM channels.
source: Therefore, TRPC6 is activated through a unique mechanism compared to TRPV and TRPM channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of agonist-binding sites across different TRP channel families.
